raw_case_text:
We report the case of an 11-year-old Nigerian boy, living in Italy since 2010. On August, 26th he flew back from a one-month stay in Nigeria, and two days later he started presenting fever. On August, 31st he complained vomiting and abdominal pain and was then conducted to the Emergency Room of our Hospital. Here, after an initial suspect of appendicitis, a diagnosis of Plasmodium falciparum malaria was made, and the patient was admitted to the Infectious Diseases ward. Body temperature was 38 C, while other vital signs were normal. His complete blood count showed leukopenia (WBC 4060, nv 4500-10800) and thrombocytopenia (PLT 59,000, nv 100,000-400,000), while hemoglobin was 13 g/dL (nv 13-16.5 g/dL). His chemistry profile showed hyperbilirubinemia (2.93 mg/dL, nv 0.2-0.5 mg/dL), AST 136 UI/L and ALT 122 UI/L (nv 13-51 UI/L and 15-47 UI/L, respectively), creatinine was 1.06 mg/dL (nv 0.3-0.9 mg/dL) and an increase of LDH values (657 U/L) was present (nv 120-330 U/L); C-reactive protein was 85.6 mg/L (nv <5 mg/L). He started therapy with piperachin/diidroartemisin 320/40 mg, 3 tablets qd, and as long as he kept presenting well-localized right upper quadrant abdominal pain, an ultrasound (US) was performed on September, 1st. The exam showed a starred sky appearance of the liver associated with a slightly enlarged gallbladder, with transonic content and thickened walls, suggestive of cholecystitis. A slight increase of the spleen's dimensions (pole-to-pole diameter 11 cm) was present, and in its context a hypo-anechoic, inhomogeneous ovalar lesion (diameter 1.5 cm) was found, raising a diagnostic doubt (Abscess? Hematoma? Cyst?). The pediatric surgeon confirmed a non-surgical approach for cholecystitis and antibiotic therapy with piperacilline/tazobactam 4.5 g tid (body weight of 42 Kg) was undertaken. As long as he kept presenting fever (Figure 1) although therapy for malaria was considered over (piperachin/diidroartemisin 320/40 mg, 3 tablets qd, from August, 31st to September, 2nd) and hemoscopy resulted negative, as suggested by the radiologist, the next day the US was repeated, showing multiple splenic abscesses. Therefore, serologies for Bartonella, Echinococcus and Entamoeba and blood cultures were sent.
Quantiferon test and coproparasitologic exam were executed, resulting both negative. An echocardiogram showed no endocarditic vegetations. On September, 5th the boy was transferred to the Pediatrics ward for cholecystitis and splenic abscesses. Antimicrobial spectrum was broadened with Claritromicine 250 mg bid per os. Blood tests were performed, including peripheral blood smear, quantitative Ig, total IgE, lymphocyte typing, hemoglobin electrophoresis and dihydrorhodamine 123 test, in order to evaluate any underlying hematologic diseases. On September, 8th, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen was performed, confirming the presence of seven focal areas of signal alteration, with prevalent peripheral subcapsular distribution (maximum size 1.7 mm).
The morphology of the formations, especially of the most voluminous, was a pyramidal wedge with the apex pointing towards the hilum, and the base of the splenic capsule, while profiles looked finely irregular (Figure 2 and 3). The radiographic appearance then made it less likely the possibility of splenic abscesses, in favour of a diagnosis of recent post-infarction outcomes or hematomas in a subacute phase. While all other requested exams resulted negative, on September, 13th, hemoglobin electrophoresis showed a percentage of HbS of 40.6%, HbA was 55.2% while HbA2 and HbF were respectively 3.5 and 0.7%. A diagnosis of SCT was then made.
On September, 15th the boy was discharged, with recommendations to radiologic follow-up and preconception counseling for him and his parents and without further antibiotic therapy.
On October, 13th the boy repeated the US, which showed a normal spleen. The timing of regression is compatible with the diagnosis of splenic infarction.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old boy presenting with fever for three days, followed by vomiting and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient returned from a 1-month stay in Nigeria on August 26 and developed a fever two days later. On August 31, he presented to the emergency room with vomiting and abdominal pain, where acute appendicitis was initially suspected. He was admitted to the hospital and continued to experience persistent fever and well-localized right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Nigerian boy living in Italy since 2010; epidemiological exposure: 1-month travel to Nigeria, returning on August 26. No prior chronic medical illnesses documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature 38.0 °C; other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed well-localized right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: WBC 4,060/mm3 (reference 4,500-10,800/mm3), platelets 59,000/mm3 (reference 100,000-400,000/mm3), hemoglobin 13 g/dL (reference 13-16.5 g/dL). Chemistry: Total bilirubin 2.93 mg/dL (reference 0.2-0.5 mg/dL), AST 136 UI/L (reference 13-51 UI/L), ALT 122 UI/L (reference 15-47 UI/L), serum creatinine 1.06 mg/dL (reference 0.3-0.9 mg/dL), LDH 657 U/L (reference 120-330 U/L), C-reactive protein 85.6 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L). Blood cultures were negative. Serologies for Bartonella, Echinococcus, and Entamoeba were negative. Quantiferon test and stool coproparasitologic examination were negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram: No endocarditic vegetations. Hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbS 40.6%, HbA 55.2%, HbA2 3.5%, HbF 0.7% (confirming sickle cell trait). Abdominal ultrasound (September 1): Starred sky appearance of the liver, slightly enlarged gallbladder with transonic content and thickened walls suggestive of acalculous cholecystitis, slight splenomegaly (pole-to-pole diameter 11 cm) with a 1.5 cm hypo-anechoic inhomogeneous ovalar splenic lesion. Repeat ultrasound (September 2): Multiple hypoechoic splenic lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal MRI (September 8): Seven focal areas of signal alteration with prevalent peripheral subcapsular distribution (maximum size 1.7 mm) demonstrating pyramidal wedge morphology with apex towards hilum and base at capsule, consistent with recent splenic infarction or subacute hematomas.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute splenic infarction and acalculous cholecystitis in a child with newly recognized sickle cell trait (SCT). Appendicitis, infective endocarditis, and other parasitic/bacterial etiologies (Bartonella, Echinococcus, Entamoeba, tuberculosis) were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Treated for malaria with oral piperaquine/dihydroartemisinin 320/40 mg (3 tablets once daily for 3 days, August 31 to September 2), achieving negative hemoscopy. Cholecystitis and splenic infarction were managed conservatively without surgery, receiving IV piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g three times daily (weight 42 kg) and oral clarithromycin 250 mg twice daily. Discharged on September 15 without antibiotics, with recommendations for preconception counseling and follow-up imaging. Follow-up abdominal ultrasound on October 13 confirmed complete resolution with a normal spleen.
